claims.text: The proposed model separately calculates phonon and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model can accurately reproduce temperature-dependent thermal-conductivity trends from 200 to 1200 K.
The proposed model can predict independently determined lattice thermal conductivity with less than 30% error.
Earlier models for this problem assumed perfect, defect-free crystals.
Keeping oxygen below 0.1 wt.% will make bulk HfNbTaTiZr microstructurally close to the idealized crystal used in DFT simulations.
DFT-derived force constants can be used to calculate the phonon contribution to thermal conductivity.
Independent electron-scattering and band-structure models can calculate the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity.
The separately calculated phonon and electronic contributions can be combined to predict total thermal conductivity.
Comparing samples with below 0.1 wt.% oxygen and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen will reveal sensitivity to impurities and defects.
A defect-scarce microstructure minimizes scattering from extrinsic defects and oxygen-related sites.
A defect-scarce microstructure makes the calculated force constants and electron-scattering rates valid for the sample.
Decoupling phonon and electronic transport accounts more precisely for mass and force-constant variation and temperature-dependent electron scattering.
Separating phonon and electronic transport yields more reliable predictions when the two contributions are similar in magnitude and sensitive to defect levels.
Lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are of similar magnitude near the low-temperature regime.
For HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, total thermal conductivity is 10–17 W/(K·m) between 300 and 1200 K.
Previous analytical estimates based on defect-free DFT and Debye-temperature approximations do not capture the separate and competing behavior of lattice and electronic heat transport.
The proposed model may require additional quantum corrections below 200 K.
Inelastic neutron scattering or Raman spectroscopy can independently determine the lattice contribution for the proposed comparison.
Hall-effect measurements can independently determine the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution for the proposed comparison.
The model should reduce prediction error by at least 30% relative to earlier models.
